summary: Describes two ways to encapsulate multiprotocol network traffic over AAL5 on ATM networks. It replaced RFC 1483.

eli5.summary: Two ways to pack different kinds of network messages into fixed-size ATM cells.

questions: how is ip carried over atm
subtitle: Two ways to carry IP, bridged Ethernet and other network traffic inside ATM's AAL5 frames.

tldr.problem: ATM moves traffic in fixed 53-octet cells, but hosts, routers and bridges need to send variable-length packets of many protocols over it, and the receiver must know which protocol each packet is.
tldr.mechanism: Packets are placed in the payload of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU. Either an LLC header (plus SNAP when needed) in front of each packet names its protocol, which allows many protocols on one virtual connection, or each virtual connection is dedicated to one protocol and carries no header.
tldr.outcome: This memo replaced RFC 1483, added a VPN identification header and security considerations, and is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 2684 is a Proposed Standard from September 1999 that obsoletes RFC 1483, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Carrying Packets Over ATM
sections.content:
ATM transports data in cells: a cell is 53 octets, made of a 5-octet header and a 48-octet payload. Variable-length packets, called PDUs here, must be cut into cell payloads by the sender and reassembled by the receiver. This memo uses AAL5 (ATM Adaptation Layer type 5) for that job, and carries routed and bridged PDUs directly in the payload of the AAL5 Common Part Convergence Sublayer (CPCS) PDU.

It defines two methods. LLC Encapsulation puts an IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control header in front of each PDU so several protocols can share one ATM virtual connection (VC). VC Multiplexing dedicates one VC to one protocol, so there is a separate VC for each protocol.

Two cases are handled elsewhere. If the Frame Relay service specific sublayer is used, RFC 2427 applies, and it MUST be used in the special case of Frame Relay Network Interworking or transparent mode Service Interworking. If you want the facilities designed for the Point-to-Point Protocol over a point-to-point relationship, RFC 2364 applies instead.
sections.eli5: ATM only sends small same-size packages. This memo explains how to put bigger messages of many kinds into those packages and have them rebuilt on the other side.

sections.title: Choosing a Multiplexing Method
sections.content:
The choice between the two methods depends on implementation and system needs. LLC encapsulation tends to need fewer VCs when several protocols are in use. VC multiplexing tends to reduce fragmentation overhead. The RFC's example is an IPv4 datagram holding a TCP control packet with no IP or TCP options, which fits exactly into a single cell.

On a Permanent Virtual Connection (PVC) the method is chosen by configuration. For Switched Virtual Connections (SVCs), ATM signalling is used to negotiate it, as specified in RFC 1755 and RFC 2331.
sections.eli5: You can either put many kinds of letters in one truck with labels, or use a different truck for each kind. For a permanent road you just agree beforehand. For a temporary road you ask when you set it up.

sections.title: The AAL5 PDU
sections.content:
Both methods put the routed or bridged PDU in the Payload field of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU. The AAL5 message mode service in the non-assured mode MUST be used, the corrupted delivery option MUST NOT be used, and a reassembly timer MAY be used.

The Payload holds up to 2^16 - 1 octets. After it come a PAD of 0 to 47 octets, which makes the trailer land at the end of the last cell, and a trailer of four fields: CPCS-UU (1 octet, unused by this memo and may be any value), CPI (1 octet, MUST be 0x00), Length (2 octets) and CRC (4 octets, a CRC-32 for detecting bit errors). A Length of 0x00 signals an abort.
sections.eli5: The message goes in a box with some filler to make it fit, and a sticker on the end that says how long the message was and lets the receiver check nothing got scrambled.

sections.title: LLC Encapsulation
sections.content:
With LLC encapsulation, the protocol of every PDU MUST be identified by an LLC header in front of it. In LLC Type 1 operation the header is three one-octet fields, DSAP, SSAP and Ctrl, and for routed protocols the Control field MUST be 0x03.

Routed protocols. The LLC value 0xFE-FE-03 marks a PDU in the ISO NLPID format, followed by a one-octet NLPID that names the protocol. An NLPID of 0x00 MUST NOT be used. Although the NLPID 0xCC exists for IP, the NLPID format MUST NOT be used for IP. IP and other protocols use a SNAP header instead: LLC 0xAA-AA-03, then a 3-octet OUI and a 2-octet PID. With OUI 0x00-00-00 the PID is an EtherType, so an IPv4 PDU uses EtherType 0x08-00. This format is consistent with RFC 1042.

Bridged protocols. The LLC header is 0xAA-AA-03, the OUI MUST be the 802.1 code 0x00-80-C2, and the PID gives the bridged media type and whether the original frame check sequence (FCS) is kept. Padding after the PID aligns the bridged frame on a four-octet boundary, and MAC addresses keep the bit order they have on the LAN. Appendix B lists the PIDs for 802.3/Ethernet, 802.4, 802.5, FDDI, 802.6 and bridge protocol data units.

A bridge that keeps the LAN FCS in an Ethernet/802.3 frame MUST include Ethernet padding. Without the FCS it MAY include or omit padding, but on receipt it MUST be able to insert any missing padding before forwarding.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a small label at the front saying what language it is written in. The receiver reads the label and hands the message to the right helper.

sections.title: VC Multiplexing
sections.content:
With VC multiplexing, the VC itself is bound to one protocol, so no protocol identification travels in each PDU. That cuts payload overhead and can reduce per-packet processing and the number of cells needed for some lengths. For PVCs the protocol is set by configuration. For SVCs the negotiation in RFC 1755 MUST be used.

A routed PDU is the only content of the AAL5 payload. A bridged PDU uses the same formats as in LLC encapsulation, except that only the fields after the PID are included. Because there is no PID, whether the LAN FCS is present is implied by the VC, so PDUs with and without the FCS count as different protocols even for the same media type.
sections.eli5: If a whole truck only ever carries one kind of letter, you do not need a label on each letter. The truck itself tells you.

sections.title: Bridging and VPN Identification
sections.content:
A bridge with an ATM interface that links to other bridges MUST be able to flood, forward and filter bridged PDUs. Flooding means sending the PDU on each relevant VC, either by copying it or by using a point-to-multipoint VC. To forward, the bridge must tie a destination MAC address to a VC. Because configuring every address by hand is unreasonable, bridged PDUs MUST use the section 5 encapsulation so the receiving interface can learn the association dynamically.

The memo also adds an encapsulation for Virtual Private Networks over an ATM subnet. The VPN-Id of RFC 2685 is 7 octets: a 3-octet VPN-related OUI followed by a 4-octet VPN index. The VPN encapsulation header is LLC 0xAA-AA-03, OUI 0x00-00-5E, PID 0x00-08, a one-octet pad, then the OUI and index, and it is prepended to the normal LLC or VC-multiplexed format.

With VC multiplexing, the VPN may instead be fixed by ATM signalling or by administrative assignment to the interface. Then all PDUs belong to that VPN and carry no header, and a receiver that gets a VPN header anyway MAY drop it.
sections.eli5: Bridges learn who lives where by looking at the labels on arriving letters. For private networks there is an extra sticker that names which private club the letter belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any encapsulation involves trust: the receiver must believe the sender identified the protocol correctly, and there is no way to check this. The memo believes the encapsulations have no other properties an attacker could exploit, but protocols above them may face many attacks. The bridging design in section 7 has the same weaknesses as other bridging architectures.

System security can also depend on the underlying ATM network. The memo points to the ATM Forum security framework and security specification as possibly relevant.
sections.eli5: The receiver has to believe the label on each letter. Nobody can check that the label is honest.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 1483
sections.content:
RFC 2684 was written to remove anachronisms, clear up ambiguities found by implementors, and advance the work through the IETF standards track. None of the substantive changes is believed to make RFC 1483 implementations obsolete.

  • NLPID usage is clarified using RFC 2119 keywords.
  • A pointer to RFC 2364 covers PPP over ATM.
  • RFC 1755 and RFC 2331 are referenced for negotiating encapsulations.
  • AAL5 now refers to ITU-T I.363.5, and its options are selected.
  • Padding between the PID and the MAC address, MAC bit order, and Ethernet/802.3 padding are clarified.
  • The VPN encapsulation, security considerations and an appendix on applications such as Classical IP over ATM, LAN Emulation and PPP over ATM are new.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up second edition of the older rulebook. It explains unclear parts and adds a few new rules.
